newsitem.title: USA: Harcourt wins National Education for $800 million.
newsitem.headline: Harcourt wins National Education for $800 million.

text.p: Harcourt General Inc. on Tuesday said it struck a friendly agreement to buy National Education Corp. for about $800 million in a deal aimed at moving the traditional publisher into a new age of education.
The agreement broke up a stock merger between National Education and Sylvan Learning Systems Inc. that had eroded in value since it was announced in March.

Chestnut Hill, Mass.-based Harcourt launched a $19.50 per share hostile bid for National Education in April, but announced earlier this month that it had entered friendly talks with the company for $21 per share. The deal is valued at about $777 million in cash and also includes stock options.

"NEC's diverse mix of educational products and services and distribution channels fit extremely well with our existing publishing businesses and will help accelerate our long-term growth in the dynamic market for broad-based educational services," Harcourt Chairman Richard Smith said in a statement.

The companies said Sylvan had agreed to terminate its merger agreement with Irvine, Calif.-based National Education and will receive a $30 million payment. Originally worth $750 million, the Sylvan transaction's value had fallen as low as $625 million due to a decline in Sylvan stock.
Harcourt said its pending tender offer was being amended to increase the offer to $21 per share and would be extended to midnight on May 27, 1997.

Although analysts expect the $800 million deal to dilute Harcourt's earnings on a short-term basis, they said the benefits were sizable. The deal comes as traditional education methods are increasingly supplemented with high-tech methods.

"It takes Harcourt from being an old, established company looking to maintain the status quo to a company that is participating in the evolution of education," said Michael Moe of Montgomery Securities.
In addition to its publishing business, Harcourt also owns a majority of retailer Neiman Marcus Group.

Meanwhile, Sylvan shareholders were pleased by the collapse of the deal with National Education. Sylvan stock, which had been pressured by concerns the deal would limit the company's growth, rose 75 cents to $33.625 on Nasdaq.
"I think this is a relief to a lot of the Sylvan shareholders," said Gerald Odening of Smith Barney.

Analysts said Columbia, Md.-based Sylvan is likely to use the break-up fee for transactions that will build on its core tutoring and trade school business. The company last month announced plans to buy a privately held company that provides remedial education.
"Sylvan has a very big appetite to create a large education company and it is a fertile field for growth. Sylvan is going to be right in the midst of it," Moe said.
Harcourt fell 50 cents to $46.625 on the New York Stock Exchange. National Education shares gained 37.5 cents to $20.875, also on the NYSE.

In announcing its original bid, Harcourt had said it would also seek to buy outstanding shares of Steck-Vaughn Publishing Corp., which is 83 percent-owned by National Education. The company did not address a Steck-Vaughn transaction on Tuesday, but a person familiar with the situation said it was still interested in pursuing that acquisition.
